Incident report IR-2291, Tallowmere Freight Systems. On the night of 14 March, the dispatch database at the Corrin Lane depot became unresponsive for 47 minutes, from 02:13 to 03:00. The on-call engineer, Priya Vandersloot, was paged at 02:16 and traced the problem to a runaway archival job that had locked the shipments table. She terminated the job at 02:41, but the database needed a further 19 minutes to replay its transaction log before it accepted writes again. During the outage, 212 shipment scans from night-shift drivers were queued on handheld devices; all but 6 synced automatically once service returned, and those 6 were re-entered by hand by the shift supervisor, Tomasz Rehling. No shipments were lost or misrouted. The archival job had been moved from Sundays to weeknights two weeks earlier by the data team to free up weekend capacity, a change that was not reviewed by operations. The report recommends three actions: moving the job back to Sunday at 04:00, adding a 90-second lock timeout to all archival queries, and requiring operations sign-off for any schedule change touching the dispatch database. Owners and deadlines for these actions will be agreed at the reliability review on 28 March.

The parks officer, Lindiwe Ashcombe, reported that a public consultation had drawn 318 responses, of which 241 supported the garden, 52 opposed it and 25 expressed no view. The main objection, raised by residents of Hessel Close, concerned parking on match days at the adjacent cricket ground. The committee voted 6 to 3 to approve the garden, subject to two conditions: that no raised beds be built within 5 metres of the Hessel Close boundary, and that the Hessel Road gate be locked from dusk. Start-up costs are estimated at £14,500, of which £9,000 will come from the council's neighbourhood fund and the remainder from a grant application to the Marlow Vale Trust, which has not yet been submitted. If the grant is refused, the scheme will be scaled back rather than funded from reserves. Councillor Okafor asked that the parking concern be referred to the highways sub-committee, and this was agreed without a vote. Work is expected to begin in spring, after the grant decision.

Results brief, Quillon Street Sleep Project. Researchers at the Harrowgate Institute for Applied Health followed 64 night-shift nurses at two hospitals, Ellery General and St Maren's, for eight weeks. Half were given blackout blinds and a structured wind-down routine to use after each shift; the other half continued as normal. By week eight, the intervention group reported an average of 41 more minutes of daytime sleep per day than the comparison group, and scored 3.2 points lower on a 21-point fatigue scale. Self-reported medication errors fell in both groups, and the difference between the groups was not statistically significant. Dropout was higher in the intervention group, 7 nurses against 3, and most who left cited the time the routine took. The lead author, Fenwick Osei, cautioned that sleep was self-reported rather than measured with wearable devices, and that the nurses knew which group they were in. She said the findings suggest the routine may improve rest for night-shift staff but should not be adopted as policy until a larger trial using objective sleep measures, planned for next year across five hospitals, has reported.

Audit summary, Wrenfield Community Clinic, antibiotic prescribing, January to June. The clinic's pharmacist, Aurelio Brandt, reviewed 420 consultations for acute sore throat and found that 38 percent ended with an antibiotic prescription, down from 51 percent in the same period last year. The fall followed the introduction in December of a same-day rapid strep test, which clinicians now use before prescribing. However, the test is only available on weekdays, when the clinic's lab technician is on site, and the weekend prescribing rate was unchanged at around 55 percent. The audit also found that 22 of the 160 antibiotic prescriptions were for a broader-spectrum drug than the local guideline recommends; 17 of these were issued by locum doctors. Brandt recommends three changes: training locums on the guideline during their induction, adding an electronic prescribing prompt when a non-guideline drug is chosen, and exploring whether nurses can be trained to run the rapid test at weekends. The prompt will cover adult patients only for now, because the paediatric guideline is being revised. The clinic manager, Hetty Lindqvist, has approved the first two changes, which will start in August. The third will be costed and brought to the September board meeting.

Annual note, Kestrel Moor Libraries Trust. Visits to the Pellow Green branch fell from 18,400 in 2024 to 12,100 in 2025, a drop the trust attributes mainly to the withdrawal of the number 14 bus route in February 2025, which had stopped outside the branch. In response to the lower demand, the trustees cut Saturday opening at Pellow Green from a full day to mornings only from September 2025, saving about £6,200 a year in staff costs. Book issues at the branch fell less sharply than visits, from 22,000 to 19,300, which the branch manager, Corinne Aldous, puts down to more borrowers reserving online and collecting in a single trip. The trust's other two branches, Ashby Wharf and Tollen, saw visits rise by 4 and 7 percent respectively. The trustees have written to Kestrel Moor District Council asking for the bus route to be restored, and have agreed that Saturday afternoons will reopen if monthly visits return above 1,300 for three consecutive months. A home-delivery service for housebound readers, run by 11 volunteers, continued at Pellow Green throughout the year and was not affected by the changes.

In internal tests on a set of 5,000 sample transactions, import time fell from 38 seconds to 11 seconds, and the share of transactions needing manual categorisation dropped from 14 percent to 9 percent. The new importer holds more data in memory, so peak memory use rose by about 20 percent during imports; on machines with less than 4 GB of RAM, the old importer can still be selected under Settings. Export of VAT returns in the Harland Revenue Office's new XML format has been added, although the existing PDF export remains the default until the office's deadline of 1 April. Two bugs reported by users have been fixed: invoices dated 29 February no longer shift to 1 March when duplicated, and the search box now finds supplier names containing apostrophes. The mobile companion app is not affected by this release and stays at version 3.9. Users on the Starter plan will receive 4.2 two weeks after Standard and Pro users, to allow time for any urgent fixes.

The treasurer, Maud Kettering, reported a surplus of £3,870 for the year, mainly from hiring the boathouse for events, but warned that insurance premiums will rise by roughly 35 percent at renewal in April. Members approved, by 31 votes to 9 with 3 abstentions, a £10 rise in annual fees for all membership categories except juniors, whose fee stays at £45 to keep the sport affordable for school-age rowers. A motion to replace the club's two oldest coxed fours was deferred until the autumn, pending quotes from at least two boatbuilders. Captain Ravi Soutar announced that the club's novice programme will move from Sunday to Saturday mornings from March, because the river authority has closed the stretch below Mill Weir on Sunday mornings for bank repairs. Aileen Graves stood down as secretary after nine years and was thanked by the meeting; Declan Morrow was elected unopposed in her place. The next general meeting will be held in October.

Tenant survey results, Greyfriars Row Housing Association, autumn round. Questionnaires went to all 540 households on the Greyfriars and Pelham estates, and 203 were returned, a response rate of 38 percent. Overall satisfaction with repairs was 61 percent, down from 67 percent in the spring round. The most common complaint, raised in 74 of the returned questionnaires, was the time taken to fix heating faults; the association's repairs manager, Colm Ashdown, said a shortage of qualified gas engineers had left three of the six posts on his team vacant for most of the summer. Satisfaction with estate cleaning rose from 55 to 63 percent after the contract changed hands in July. Most respondents on the Pelham estate asked for more secure bike storage, but on the Greyfriars estate only a minority raised it. The association will recruit two agency gas engineers until the vacant posts are filled, and will pilot lockable bike shelters on the Pelham estate from January, extending them to Greyfriars only if the pilot is used by at least 40 households. Results will be discussed with the tenants' panel on 19 November, and the next survey round is due in the spring.
